lines.en: : An arcade? This is where you wanted to go? Why?
: Because I am a fun-loving, quirky girl on a mission to make as many memories as possible with her father before he gets too old and dies.
: Plus, I have you all to myself today and I want you to watch me wipe the floor with old people on the mahjong machines.

: This sounds like it would be a good moment to teach you to always respect your elders but, honestly, I’m just thankful to be the only senior citizen in this room that you aren’t trying to turn into a fool.
: It’s less that I’m trying to make them look like fools and more the fact that my hobbies just don’t really mesh well with other girls my age. Old people, though? They get me.
: Well, I’m glad at least someone does because I didn’t even know that you knew how to play mahjong until literally right now.
: I actually don’t. I am a liar. You have raised a rotten girl who doesn’t know how to tell the truth. I come here to smoke cigarettes and partake in underage drinking in the purikura booths.
: That’s more like it. No child of mine is going to hang out with old people. Now, let’s go get smashed and then forget to tell your mother about it.
: Finally, I get to act as a proper high school dropout and not the kind who spends most of her days watching various Netflix documentaries with her dad!
: You’ll learn more from those than you will from me. There’s nothing left for me to teach you, unfortunately.
: All part of the plan, of course. I knew what I was doing when I came to you guys about quitting school. And I regret nothing since now we get to do stuff like this during weekdays!
: Just remember that we can’t make this into a regular thing and that we’re only here because the Internet is down. I’m still giving you a quiz tomorrow.
: And I’ll still ace it because I’m the best. Which means we’ve got a full day’s worth of daddy-daughter festivities to get to before we have to think about learning at all!
: You’re right. I’ll go buy the alcohol now since you’re not legally allowed to yet.
: Sounds good, Dad! I’ll go find us an empty purikura booth to-
: AAAAAHHHH!
: What is it? You don’t see someone from school, do-
: RABBIT!
: ...Rabbit?
: This is what you were freaking out about? Why?
: Because I’ve finally found the perfect opportunity for you to prove your manliness and provide for me by satisfying the instinctive masculine urge to win crane game prizes for a cute girl!
: It is true that this is a thing I feel compelled to do. But I think that is less because you are cute and more because you are-
: The light of your life?
: Close. I was going to say, “because you are going to whine about it all day if I don’t.”
: That’s not even remotely close. Be nicer to me. Your time on this planet is limited and I’ll be reluctant to handle your funeral arrangements if you don’t make me the center of your world.
: Are you sure this is what you want? There are a bunch of other crane games around here with less, uh...vintage plushes in them.
: I have set my sights on this one. Win it for me and prove your love, Father. I have no choice but to doubt it until this object is in my hands.
: If you insist.
: Yes! Go, go, go! Do the dad thing! Get it in one shot and you might finally usurp Mom’s role as my favorite!
: I think I’ll fail for her sake then. So when I don’t get it on the first try, know that it’s because I’m just being considerate and not that I’m bad at this.

: Don’t worry, Dad. Because even if you do suck, you can still win through the act of persistence by failing so many times that an employee feels bad for you and comes over here to position the prize on the ledge.
: Are you speaking from experience here, Himawari?
: Me? Who is good at everything? Pfft. As if. There’s no way that happened to me every Wednesday after school for an entire month. I was too busy smoking cigarettes. Remember?
: And where are you getting the money for those cigarettes exactly? We don’t give you an allowance.
: I have ten online boyfriends who send me money in exchange for ASMR goodnight messages, obviously. All the girls my age are doing it, Dad. Respect the hustle.
: I’m going to need you to hand over your phone now.
: But that’s where I keep all my pictures of you! And my super secret diary about how much I love you and how awesome you are! It’d be, like, so embarrassing if you read all of that!
: Move the claw already. The timer is going to run out.
: Hi, Mom! Just checking in to make sure you’re still beautiful. And, would you look at that? You still are! Perhaps even more so than this morning.
: Thank you, Hima-chan. I needed that today and- wait, where are you right now?
: On a date with Dad. Internet went out. Look at the plushie he won me.
: I’ve decided to name him Che Guevara. And no, I will not elaborate.
: Himawari, it’s a school day. You promised that you were still going to take your education seriously after dropping out. It’s one of the main reasons we agreed to-
: I am taking it seriously! Dad’s giving me a quiz tomorrow and everything. Plus, you know what they say about mental health. I see this outing as an investment, if anything.
: Hah...Are you having fun, at least? You look cute today.
: Don’t I? I’m wearing one of your old necklaces. Which is poetic in a sense because you might have been wearing it when you created me.
: Are you two going to be home for dinner? Or should I pick something up for myself on the way home from work?
: You won’t be mad at me if I keep him all day, will you? We’re having a lot of fun and there’s somewhere else I want to go after this.
: Of course not. Just don’t stay out too late, okay?
: Yeah, yeah. You’ll get him back before bed. Don’t worry.
: Hima-chan, that’s not-
: Anyway, gotta run! Dad’s back! Love you!
: Himawari-
: End call.
: You didn’t just hang up on your mother, did you?
: It’s rude to talk on the phone during a date.
: It’s rude to talk on the phone in a restaurant either way. But I think hanging up on one’s mother might trump that.
: What’s done is done. Now, what is the bountiful feast you have prepared for us today? Chicken skewers and onigiri, I see. But what rests within these balls of rice, I wonder?
: Ume for both. They didn’t have ikura, unfortunately.
: I accept this compromise for ume is my second favorite fish.
: Your second favorite fish is a plum?
: That shouldn’t come as that big of a surprise considering my first favorite is an egg.
: Is that beer for me? Thanks, Dad!
: Drink your soda. This is mine. You’re forbidden from partaking outside of photo booths.
: I accept this compromise for Coca Cola is my third favorite fish.
: I really wonder how you turned out like this. Your mother’s weirdness only manifested in her just always having a gun for some reason.
: Seriously? Who does that?
: Himawari, put that down.
: Already? But I just met him...
: Himawari...
: Look out over the river and picture it, Lennie...
: I thought you named the rabbit Che Guevara?

: I did. But I wasn’t about to pass up an opportunity to add some aesthetic irony to a classic novel. Lennie being a rabbit would have made imagining other rabbits a little more poignant, don’t you think?
: Plus, Che Guevara was killed by a gunshot wound and I didn’t want to potentially upset any Cuban revolutionaries in the room.
: Fair enough. There are a lot of those in Aomori.
: Sure are, Dad. But winter is just around the corner at this point and I’m sure they’ll all go back into hiding soon enough. It gets way colder here than it does in Cuba.
: On that note, are you excited for Hokkaido? It’s right around the corner at this point.
: Heck yeah, I am! Mom said she’s finally going to teach me how to ski!
: I didn’t even realize she knew how to ski. But she comes from a rich family, so I guess it makes sense.
: Did you ever get to meet Grandpa before he died, Dad? Or did you sort of avoid that drama on account of being an adult who impregnated his teenage daughter?
: I never really had any desire to. Your mom never had much nice to say about him after the whole bubble wrap thing took off.
: Still crazy that’s what killed him in the end. Who’d have thought that even unpoppable bubble wrap is poppable with enough force?
: Well, we certainly know who wouldn’t. Now, eat your food before it gets cold.
: Fine, fine. Thanks for looking out for me, Dad. I- mnghhhfpphffhpphh?!??!! This isn’t ume at all! Is this...mngh! This onigiri is just filled with wasabi!
: You are not the only one here who doesn’t know how to tell the truth, Himawari. Your father is just as rotten as you are.
: Mmmmmmnghhh!!!! I really am calling CPS this time!!!!!
The two of us gorge ourselves on food that Ayane only seldom allows in the house, taking our time to savor each and every bite since we know that moments like this are rare.
And that sooner or later, they’ll be little more than a thing of the past. Once our bodies start becoming less tolerant of sodium and fat and even time itself.
It’s things like this that make it easier to get lost in a moment — so immersed in now that the mere idea of “later” is an entirely foreign concept.
I’m starting to wish things would stay that way.
Every day, it seems less likely that I’ll be leaving this place.
That, somehow or another, this girl did save me when she ushered us through a door on that rooftop months ago.
Which means that time is moving again. The weather is changing and I am getting older. She is getting older.
The years will go by and I will see her less and less as they do. And, one day, she’ll have a family of her own to merge into mine.
I’m sure we’ll spend Christmases together since Ayane loves them so much. I’m excited to see if Himawari is the same.
But I want it to end there for I am once again afraid of the passage of time now that I’ve been reminded of how it feels.
I am afraid that one day I will wake up and I won’t hear her footsteps anymore. That she’ll stop teasing me and begin to scorn me for my reluctance to let her go.
I’m afraid of a world in which she sees my name appear on her phone and doesn’t pick up on the first ring. Buying fewer groceries. What to do with her room when she moves out.
It’s funny, though.
Because I used to think I was afraid of everything...but it wasn’t until I met her that those fears multiplied by a number so large I can’t even properly think it.
So maybe it wasn’t ever fear at all back then. And maybe it was something else.
That all seems so distant now, though.
: Do you ever wish you could just, like...stop the clock? And live in a single moment for the rest of your life?
: Yeah...
: I think we all do sometimes.
: Do you feel that way right now?
: Do you?
: I asked you first.
: Yeah. But my answer is embarrassing, so I want you to go.
: So is mine! And you’re the adult here, so I think you should be the one setting an example.
: Then yes. I do feel that way right now.
: I feel it every moment I look at you.
: Wow. That is embarrassing.
: I told you.
: You think Mom is the same way?
: I know she’s the same way.
: You know that, before you were born, she used to talk about wanting a ton of children? Like...a staggering amount of them.
: And she called it quits after just one? Was I that much of a terror as a baby?
: The opposite. I think she just loved you so much that the idea of having to split that love seemed unfair to you.
: Do you think I’d make a good sister?
: I think you’d make a good anything. Which is why I live each day in an incessant state of shock now.
: To think that you came from me, just...
: I can’t comprehend it.
: You’re pretty great too, you know.
: Maybe not back in the day. But I didn’t know you then, so all I can really do is judge you based on now.  On what I have seen.
: I don’t want to grow up.
: You’re going to have to.
: Are you guys going to kick me out when I turn eighteen?
: Probably not. But I think you’re too smart to let yourself grow old in our house. And that you’ll eventually want to leave if you don’t already.
: What does being smart have to do with a person’s feelings? I can be a genius and still not want to leave your side.
: You could. But then the world would miss out on someone who could change it for the better.
: Well, maybe I’m just an asshole then. Because I don’t really care about other people.
: Finally, you take after me in some way. And here I thought you were just a newer version of your mom.
: Oh yeah? No wonder why you love me so much.
: I’d still love you even if you were nothing like her.
: You mean it?
: I do.
: You really are the light of my life.
: I can’t explain how much you’ve changed me in such a short amount of time.
: Can you try? I like it when you compliment me. It feels like I’m being wrapped in a big, warm dad-blanket.
: I’ve already told you I love you and that’s taxing enough as someone who never learned how to properly express himself.
: I don’t think it’s too late to learn if you really try. Mom always says I get you closer to smiling than anybody else. That’s a good first step, isn’t it?
: You don’t want me to get better at expressing myself. You’d literally never hear the end of it.
: I wouldn’t need to if I could stop the clock.
: I could listen to you...and look at you forever. And if you ever need to catch your breath, you can let me pick up the slack so I can try to express myself too.
: I’m probably worse at it than you think, though. I’m just not as good at finding the right words as you.
: Well, your mom’s also the type to let her actions speak louder than those. There are just two different types of people, I guess.
: I hope I can make you understand one day...just how much you really mean to me.
: You will.
: I already know it.
: I just don’t think it’s really hit me yet.
: Well, when it does, can you let me know? Because giving 100%% every minute of every day sounds like it could get exhausting.
: And sometimes, it’s nice to just sit back and relax with someone you love. Right, Dad?
: Right...
: The view from here is beautiful, isn’t it?
: Yeah...
: It really is.
